requirements.requirement: Enable a persistent (boot-surviving) host firewall on node1
requirements.summary: ufw was configured and enabled with 'ufw --force enable' returning 'Firewall is active and enabled on system startup'; systemctl is-enabled/is-active confirmed 'enabled'/'active' both before and after a real reboot (boot_id changed from fa1e87e6... to aa6782c3..., matching the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots). Post-restart check shows ufw still active with the same rules and default-deny policy intact.

ufw-user-input chain shows an explicit ACCEPT for tcp dpt:22 on the real ens2 interface, both immediately after configuration and after the reboot; sshd remained listening and reachable (the post-restart poll itself succeeded via SSH).
ufw-user-input chain shows an explicit ACCEPT for tcp dpt:8080, present both pre- and post-reboot.

Default incoming policy set to deny, INPUT chain policy is DROP, and ufw-user-input only contains ACCEPT rules for 22/tcp and 8080/tcp (loopback and ESTABLISHED/RELATED separately allowed as expected). Post-restart INPUT chain already shows 3 dropped packets since boot, confirming active enforcement. Note: ufw's default behavior is a silent DROP rather than an explicit TCP RST/ICMP REJECT, so if 'rejecting' was meant literally as an active reject response this is a minor semantic gap, though 'deny unrelated traffic' is the standard and commonly accepted interpretation of such firewall requirements.

overall_summary: The executor configured ufw on node1 with a default-deny-incoming policy, explicit allow rules for 22/tcp and 8080/tcp, and enabled it for boot persistence. iptables inspection directly shows the ufw-user-input chain only accepts the two intended ports, and a full reboot cycle (pre-restart baseline, disconnection, changed boot_id, and post-restart re-verification) confirms the firewall configuration and SSH access both survived the restart, satisfying the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol as well as the task's persistence requirement. The main blemish is an unreverted netcat-openbsd package install used for a flawed same-host connectivity test that the executor itself discarded in favor of direct rule inspection.
limitations: No connectivity test from a genuinely external host/network was captured; the executor's same-host nc test was invalid due to loopback routing and was correctly discarded, so enforcement is demonstrated only via local iptables/ufw rule inspection rather than an end-to-end network probe.

ufw's default policy is a silent DROP rather than an active REJECT; if the task's use of 'rejecting' implied TCP RST/ICMP responses rather than generic denial, this would be a partial gap, though DROP is the standard interpretation for this kind of requirement.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were purposeful (ufw configuration) or properly reverted (temporary nc listeners on 8080/9999 for a connectivity test, started in cmd-a7069b93005f4e2e and fully killed/cleaned in cmd-b8571ee7383e4800). One unnecessary and unreverted mutation: cmd-39c4db3202124156 installed the netcat-openbsd package via apt-get to support a same-host connectivity test that the executor itself later recognized was invalid (self-directed traffic routes via loopback, which ufw always accepts, so even the unrelated port 9999 falsely appeared reachable). The package was left installed with no cleanup and was not used in the final evidence set, making it a low-risk but unnecessary residual mutation not tied to a material outcome. An earlier reboot attempt without sudo (cmd-d053eb0e5c2144d5) failed with a permission error and had no effect on system state, so it is not counted as a harmful mutation.
